summary: Describes changes to several TLS and DTLS IANA registries, from adding notes to altering registration policy. Most were motivated by a working group review of these registries during the TLS 1.3 development process, and the document updates a number of earlier RFCs.

eli5.summary: TLS keeps official lists of names and numbers. After tidying up, this note fixes some entries and changes who may add new ones.

subtitle: A housekeeping pass over the TLS and DTLS IANA registries: looser rules for new entries, a Recommended column and clearer warnings.

tldr.problem: After the working group reviewed the TLS and DTLS IANA registries during TLS 1.3 development, several had names, policies or notes that no longer fit. Some policies were too strict, and some readers treated the registries as checklists of what to implement.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC tells IANA to rename registries, switch several to Specification Required with a Private Use range, add a Recommended column, and attach warnings and notes. It also sets up a designated expert review process.
tldr.outcome: New TLS extensions, cipher suites and similar entries are easier to register, while the Recommended column shows which entries the IETF generally recommends. RFC 9847 later updated this document.

today: RFC 8447 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9847. It updates RFCs 3749, 4680, 5077, 5246, 5705, 5878, 6520 and 7301.

sections.title: Why the Registries Changed
sections.content:
RFC 8447 records changes that IANA made to a number of registries for Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS). The changes were almost entirely motivated by the development of TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446), and they range from simple, such as adding notes, to complex, such as changing a registry's registration policy.

The document does not change the policies for the TLS Alerts, ContentType, HandshakeType and Certificate Status Types registries. Standards Action stays for the first three and IETF Review for the last, because one-byte code points are scarce.
sections.eli5: Imagine a club keeps a sign-up book. After a big event the organisers tidy the book and change a few of the sign-up rules.

sections.title: Renames and Policy Alignment
sections.content:
For consistency, IANA prepended TLS to four registry names: the Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) Protocol IDs, ExtensionType Values, Heartbeat Message Types and Heartbeat Modes. Entry 35 in the extension registry was renamed session_ticket, and entry 4 in the HandshakeType registry was renamed new_session_ticket, so names match the presentation language field names.

Many registries used the procedure "IETF Consensus", which RFC 8126 renamed to "IETF Review". IANA updated the TLS Authorization Data Formats and TLS Supplemental Data Formats registries accordingly. This was not a universal change, since other registries were changing in other ways.

Entry 120, no_application_protocol, was also added to the TLS Alerts registry, because it was left out of the IANA instructions in RFC 7301.
sections.eli5: Some labels in the book got clearer names, and one entry that was forgotten was written in.

sections.title: Looser Policies and a Recommended Column
sections.content:
Experience showed that the old IETF Review or IETF Consensus policies were too strict for extensions, cipher suites, ClientCertificateType identifiers and certificate types. These now use Specification Required. For ExtensionType and Cipher Suites, values with a first byte of 0 to 254 use Specification Required and first byte 255 is Private Use. ClientCertificateType values 0 to 63 need Standards Action, 64 to 223 need Specification Required, and 224 to 255 are Private Use. Certificate Types 0 to 223 need Specification Required and 224 to 255 are Private Use.

A new Recommended column marks parameters that are generally recommended for implementations to support. The default is N. Adding a Y requires Standards Action, and moving from Y to N requires IESG Approval. An N does not mean an item is flawed; it may not have been through the IETF consensus process, may have limited applicability, or may be for specific use cases.

The column was added to many registries, including extensions, cipher suites, supported groups, exporter labels and certificate types.
sections.eli5: The rules for adding to the book got easier, with a small corner left for private use. A Y sticker marks the entries the experts suggest.

sections.title: Cipher Suites, Groups and Exporter Labels
sections.content:
The Cipher Suites registry marks as Y a list of Standards Track TLS 1.2 suites, such as TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, plus a list of ephemeral pre-shared key suites. The TLS 1.3 suites get their status from RFC 8446. CCM_8 suites are not marked Recommended because of their significantly truncated authentication tag.

In the Supported Groups registry, secp256r1, secp384r1, x25519 and x448 are marked Y and the rest N. The value 0 (0x0000) is reserved.

The TLS Exporter Labels registry gets a note that RFC 5705 defined exporters using the TLS PRF while RFC 8446 replaced the PRF with HKDF. The exporter interface is the same but the value is computed differently. The designated expert also checks that a label is printable ASCII beginning with EXPORTER, and IANA must verify that no label is a prefix of another.
sections.eli5: The strongest, most trusted choices get a Y. Labels must not start the same way as other labels, so nothing gets mixed up.

sections.title: Warnings and Orphaned Registries
sections.content:
Some customers use the IANA registry as a checklist of implementation completeness, and some implementers blindly implement cipher suites. The RFC calls this misguided and has IANA add a WARNING that cryptographic algorithms will be broken or weakened over time and that blindly implementing listed items is not advised. The warning appears on the Cipher Suites, Supported Groups and SignatureScheme registries, and on the HashAlgorithm and SignatureAlgorithm registries.

A note on the Cipher Suites registry explains that TLS 1.3 uses the same space but defines suites differently: they specify only the symmetric ciphers and hash function. TLS 1.2 and lower suites cannot be used with TLS 1.3, and the reverse.

Registries that (D)TLS 1.3 orphaned are annotated as applying only to versions before 1.3. These include HashAlgorithm, SignatureAlgorithm and ClientCertificateType. In the Compression Method Identifiers registry, only value 0 (NULL) applies to 1.3 or later.
sections.eli5: A warning sticker says: do not copy every item in the list without thinking, because some of them get weak over time. Old pages are marked as only for older versions.

sections.title: The Designated Expert Pool
sections.content:
Specification Required requests are registered after a three-week review on the tls-reg-review@ietf.org mailing list, on the advice of one or more designated experts. The experts may approve early if they are satisfied a specification will be published. Their job is to ensure the specification is publicly available. An Internet-Draft or a document from another standards body, industry consortium or university site is enough. Their approval is not an endorsement.

Experts either approve or deny within the review period. Denials SHOULD include an explanation. Requests undetermined for longer than 21 days can be raised with the IESG. Criteria include whether the proposal duplicates existing functionality, is of general applicability and has a clear description. IANA MUST only accept updates from the designated experts, and multiple experts representing different applications are suggested.
sections.eli5: A small panel of helpers checks each new entry. They make sure it is written down somewhere public, and they answer within a few weeks.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Moving from IETF Review to Specification Required lowers the amount of review the working group gives to cipher suites and supported groups. The RFC says this reflects reality, since the working group essentially provided no cryptographic review of them, especially national cipher suites.

Recommended algorithms are regarded as secure for general use at the time of registration, but the Recommended status may lag behind advances in cryptanalysis. Expert review is not an endorsement. The IANA Considerations section simply says the document is entirely about changes to TLS-related registries.
sections.eli5: Easier sign-up means fewer people double-check each new entry, so readers still need to check that an item is safe before using it.
